title: Python structure that keeps experiments understandable
summary: Use classes, decorators, generators, and modules to separate model state from experimental procedure.

sections.title: Organize around responsibilities
paragraphs: A research script quickly accumulates data handling, model construction, training, and evaluation. Classes help when an object must keep state together with behavior: a dataset owns indexing rules, while a model owns parameters. Functions remain a better fit for stateless transformations. Modules divide those responsibilities into importable files, making it possible to test a data transformation or reuse an evaluation routine without launching an entire training run.

sections.title: Understand the control flow
paragraphs: A generator yields one item at a time and preserves its local execution state between yields. It suits streaming data that should not be materialized at once, but a consumed generator is not automatically reusable. A decorator receives a function and returns a replacement, often adding logging or a context. When wrapping functions, preserve metadata with functools.wraps. These mechanisms are ordinary Python execution, so debug them independently before hiding them inside training abstractions.

sections.title: Avoid surprising import-time behavior
paragraphs: Importing a module executes its top-level statements. Creating a large dataset, connecting a tracker, or starting training during import makes reuse fragile and can interact badly with worker processes. Put the experiment entry point behind the main guard. Keep mutable per-instance state inside initialization rather than as a shared class attribute. Record configuration explicitly instead of relying on whichever global variable was last assigned in an interactive notebook.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the Python class and module tutorials as descriptions of execution and ownership, rather than as a list of syntax features. In RunningMean, total and count belong to each instance because initialization assigns them through self. Create two instances, update only one, and compare their values. This small example exposes the same ownership distinction that matters when several experiments construct datasets, models, or metric accumulators in one process.

The language reference is the appropriate source for decorator behavior. A decorated definition binds the result of applying the decorator, so a wrapper can change call behavior even when the function's visible name stays familiar. Separately, a generator preserves one suspended computation; creating another generator object starts another computation. These are different mechanisms. When training unexpectedly begins during import or an epoch contains no batches, trace ordinary Python execution before investigating framework internals.

exercise.prompt: A generator yields three batches. You loop through it for epoch one and reuse the same generator object for epoch two. Why are there no batches, and what should change?
exercise.answer: The first pass exhausted the generator. Call a generator-producing function again for each epoch, or use a reusable iterable whose iteration method creates a fresh iterator. Resetting an epoch counter alone does not reset generator state.

takeaways: Make state ownership explicit.
Imports should define reusable components without starting experiments.

title: The shell is part of your experiment
summary: Treat paths, processes, and environment variables as reproducibility inputs rather than background details.

sections.title: A command runs inside an environment
paragraphs: The same training command can behave differently because its working directory, executable path, environment variables, or available files differ. Relative paths are resolved from the process's working directory, not necessarily from the source file's location. A useful experiment record therefore includes the command, environment configuration, and dataset location. This makes debugging an absent checkpoint or unexpected Python installation far more concrete than repeatedly editing the model.

sections.title: Understand process inheritance
paragraphs: A shell starts child processes with an inherited environment. Exported variables become available to those children; an ordinary unexported shell variable generally does not. A child process cannot modify its parent's environment just by assigning a variable. Standard output and standard error are separate streams, which lets you save ordinary progress and diagnostic failures independently. The exit code is another output: zero conventionally indicates success, while a nonzero code should stop dependent pipeline steps.

sections.title: Inspect before changing anything
paragraphs: Start with read-only observations: print the working directory, inspect the selected Python executable, list expected files, and check whether a training process is still alive. Quote paths containing spaces and avoid relying on interactive shell initialization in automated jobs. A process that disappears after a remote terminal closes may need a session manager or job scheduler. Environment variables are also a poor place to print indiscriminately, because they can contain credentials unrelated to the experiment.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: The Bash Environment manual explains which assignments are inherited by an external command. Relate its examples to a concrete training launch: an exported DATA_ROOT and an unexported local variable can look equally visible inside the shell, yet only the exported value ordinarily appears in the Python process environment. A command-prefixed assignment is another route for supplying that one child's environment without permanently changing the shell's value.

The important boundary is between processes, not between files. A child that changes its own environment does not thereby rewrite its parent's state. This also explains why running an activation script as a separate process can differ from evaluating it inside the current shell. The syntax in this article is specifically Bash syntax; PowerShell uses different environment-assignment commands. Preserve the conceptual distinction while translating commands for the actual shell, and inspect the selected executable before assuming an environment change took effect.

exercise.prompt: A Bash script sets DATA_ROOT=/datasets but launches Python without exporting it. Python cannot read DATA_ROOT from its environment. Give two ways to make the variable available.
exercise.answer: Use export DATA_ROOT=/datasets before launching Python, or prefix that one invocation with DATA_ROOT=/datasets python train.py. The second form limits the assignment to the invoked command's environment and its descendants.

takeaways: Working directory and environment affect reproducibility.
Child processes inherit exported state, not arbitrary parent variables.

title: Git records experimental decisions as reviewable changes
summary: Use commits, branches, merges, and pull requests to preserve the reasoning behind code changes.

sections.title: A commit is a meaningful checkpoint
paragraphs: Git stores a history of source snapshots, making it possible to compare an experiment with its baseline and recover the exact implementation that produced a result. A useful commit groups one coherent change and explains its purpose. An experiment log should record the commit identifier alongside configuration and data version; otherwise a saved checkpoint may outlive the code needed to interpret it.

sections.title: Separate working files from recorded history
paragraphs: Edits first exist in the working tree. Staging selects which changes enter the next commit, so a commit need not contain every current edit. A branch is a movable reference to a line of commits. Merging combines histories and may require resolving incompatible edits to the same context. A pull request adds a review and discussion workflow around proposed changes; it is a hosting-platform concept, not a special kind of Git commit.

sections.title: Review the diff that will actually be committed
paragraphs: Before committing, inspect both unstaged and staged differences. A forgotten configuration change or generated result can silently alter reproducibility. Keep large model weights and secrets out of ordinary repository history; store versioned artifact references instead. Resolve merge conflicts by understanding the intended behavior from both branches, then run the relevant check. Choosing all changes from one side merely to remove conflict markers can erase an experiment's essential logic.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read Pro Git's discussion of recording changes with three versions of one file in mind: the last commit, the staged snapshot, and the current working copy. After staging a file and editing it again, the second edit belongs only to the working copy until it is included by staging or a commit mode that reads tracked working files. Comparing the two diffs explains why a plain commit can contain an earlier version of a file that looks different in the editor.

For an experiment, a commit identifier is useful evidence but not a complete environment description. Uncommitted changes, dataset revisions, downloaded weights, and runtime arguments can still alter the result. Connect the recorded source snapshot to those external inputs through the experiment record. When reviewing a merge, follow the behavior that each branch intended to preserve; syntactically resolving a conflict is insufficient if the resulting model or data pipeline now combines incompatible assumptions.

exercise.prompt: You stage train.py, then edit it again before committing. Which version enters the commit? How can you verify the answer before committing?
exercise.answer: With a plain git commit, the staged snapshot enters the commit while later edits remain in the working tree. Inspect git diff --staged to see that snapshot and git diff for unstaged edits. By contrast, git commit -a includes current changes to tracked files, and git commit train.py records that named tracked file’s current contents rather than its earlier staged version.

takeaways: A commit records the staged snapshot.
Link code revisions to configurations, data, and results.

title: Tensor transformations should preserve the meaning of each axis
summary: Distinguish reshaping storage from reordering dimensions and use einsum to name contractions.

sections.title: Shape changes are not interchangeable
paragraphs: A tensor is an array plus metadata such as shape, strides, dtype, and device. Reshape changes how elements are grouped into dimensions while preserving their logical order. Permute reorders axes, changing which coordinate refers to which semantic role. These operations can produce the same final shape but different values in each position. In sequence models, confusing them can mix tokens, heads, and features without producing a runtime error.

sections.title: Split heads, then reorder them
paragraphs: Start with a projected tensor shaped \([B,T,H\cdot D]\). Reshape it to \([B, T, H, D]\), then permute to \([B, H, T, D]\) for attention. The first operation splits a feature axis; the second moves the head axis. Einsum can make a contraction explicit: 'btd,dh->bth' projects features while retaining batch and time. With an explicit output, dimensions whose labels are omitted from that output are summed, whether or not a label repeats across operands. Repeating a label within one operand selects its diagonal; for example, 'ii->i' extracts a diagonal without summing it.

sections.title: Views share data, copies do not
paragraphs: Some transformations return a view into existing storage, so changing one tensor can affect another. A permuted tensor is often noncontiguous; view may then reject a requested layout, while reshape may allocate a copy. Do not assume reshape is always free. Inspect shape and stride, and use tiny tensors filled with distinct sequential values to see whether a transformation preserves the intended token order. Performance decisions come after this semantic check.
sections.code:
x = torch.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)
y = x.permute(0, 2, 1)
print(x.shape, y.shape)
print(y[0, 0])  # original feature 0 across three positions

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the Tensor Views reference to inspect shape and stride together. The sequential-value tensor in this article makes a permutation observable: y[0, 0] contains original feature zero across positions, rather than an arbitrary group of three adjacent values. A view can share storage while changing indexing, and a reshape can copy when the requested arrangement is incompatible with existing strides. Similar shapes therefore do not imply identical storage or semantics.

The einsum reference makes a second distinction explicit. In ij->i, j is summed even though it appears only once in the input notation. In ii->i, repeating i within the matrix selects the diagonal and the output retains that index. Compare both examples with matrix multiplication before using a compact contraction in attention. The output labels specify which named axes survive; they are part of the computation, not an optional description added afterward.

exercise.prompt: A tensor has shape \([2, 5, 24]\) with 3 attention heads. Give the reshape and permutation needed for head dimension 8.
exercise.answer: First reshape to \([2, 5, 3, 8]\). Then permute axes as \((0, 2, 1, 3)\), producing \([2, 3, 5, 8]\). A single reshape directly to the final shape would generally assign different values to head and token positions.

takeaways: Reshape splits or combines axes; permute moves them.
Validate transformations using identifiable values, not shape alone.

title: Broadcasting and batched matrix multiplication solve different problems
summary: Learn when dimensions are expanded and when they are contracted in PyTorch operations.

sections.title: Expansion does not imply reduction
paragraphs: Elementwise broadcasting repeats a compatible pattern across larger axes without summing anything. Matrix multiplication instead contracts an inner dimension by summing products. Both may operate on batches, which is why their shape rules can look similar. Keep the two steps separate: first identify any batch axes that broadcast, then identify the matrix dimensions whose inner sizes must match.

sections.title: Work through a batched attention product
paragraphs: Let \(Q\) have shape \([4, 2, 7, 8]\) and \(K\) have shape \([4, 2, 9, 8]\), representing batch, heads, positions, and head features. Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) produces \([4, 2, 7, 9]\). The final feature dimension contracts. By contrast, multiplying \(Q\) by a scale of shape \([8]\) is elementwise and preserves \([4, 2, 7, 8]\). A scale of \([2]\) does not automatically select the head axis; it aligns with the last axis and fails here.

sections.title: Use explicit singleton dimensions
paragraphs: To scale each head separately, reshape head weights to \([1, 2, 1, 1]\). This states exactly where variation is allowed. Broadcasting often avoids allocating repeated inputs, but the resulting output can still be huge: comparing all pairs of \(B\) examples creates \(B^2\) entries. In-place operations are more restrictive because the destination cannot change shape. Prefer small shape assertions and a hand-calculated batch before optimizing a complicated contraction.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the broadcasting rules alongside the tensor tutorial's distinction between elementwise and matrix products. For the attention example, separate the leading \([4, 2]\) batch/head dimensions from the final matrix dimensions before multiplying. The inner feature width 8 is contracted, while the two position lengths 7 and 9 remain. Replacing the matrix product with elementwise multiplication would not express the same comparisons, even if selected input dimensions happened to match.

A per-head scale is a useful diagnostic because its intended semantics are easy to state: all positions and features within one head receive the same multiplier. The shape \([1, 2, 1, 1]\) records exactly that policy. If a future model happens to have feature width 2, the incorrect shape \([2]\) might stop raising an error while still scaling features instead of heads. Test deliberately unequal dimensions to avoid letting coincidences conceal an axis mistake.

exercise.prompt: \(X\) is \([3, 5, 4]\) and \(W\) is \([1, 4, 6]\). What is \(X\mathbin{@}W\)? What shape should a per-example scalar have to multiply that result?
exercise.answer: The product has shape \([3, 5, 6]\): \(W\)'s batch dimension broadcasts across three examples. Per-example scalars should have shape \([3, 1, 1]\), so each scalar is shared across positions and output features.

takeaways: Broadcasting aligns trailing axes.
Matrix multiplication contracts features while broadcasting batch dimensions.

title: Autograd follows the computation you actually executed
summary: Understand dynamic graphs, leaf gradients, and the difference between tracking gradients and using them.

sections.title: The graph is a record of operations
paragraphs: PyTorch records differentiable operations involving tensors that require gradients. The resulting graph connects a scalar loss back to parameters through the operations used in that forward pass. Python control flow can change this graph from one iteration to the next. Autograd differentiates the implemented computation faithfully; if the code uses the wrong target or a misplaced detach, a successful backward call will not correct the mathematical mistake.

sections.title: Backward accumulates into leaves
paragraphs: A parameter is typically a leaf tensor, and its gradient is accumulated in .grad when backward runs. Calling backward again without clearing gradients adds to the existing value. Intermediate tensors usually do not retain .grad unless requested. Most saved forward intermediates are released after backward, which saves memory. Keeping a graph alive intentionally is useful for some higher-order calculations, but retain_graph should not be a routine fix for a misunderstood training loop.

sections.title: Know which actions break the path
paragraphs: Calling detach creates a tensor disconnected from the current gradient history. Converting a value to a Python scalar with item removes its differentiable connection too. A no_grad context avoids recording operations, making it useful for evaluation or parameter updates. Setting model.eval() changes certain layer behaviors but does not disable autograd. Verify one parameter gradient against a hand derivation before relying on a large training system.
sections.code:
x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x * x + 3 * x
y.backward()
print(x.grad)  # 7

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: The autograd tutorial distinguishes recording a computation from updating parameters. Use the small polynomial here to follow that boundary: backward produces the derivative 7 at \(x = 2\), but \(x\) itself remains 2 until some update changes it. Repeated backward calls from independent computations add contributions into the leaf gradient. Inspect the parameter value and its gradient separately to avoid mistaking successful differentiation for successful learning.

Trace detach and no_grad through the same example. A detached value can still participate in later differentiable work with other parameters, but it no longer carries a path back through the original history. Evaluation mode is a separate switch that affects selected modules' behavior. This distinction is useful when reading saliency or attribution code: evaluating a model and differentiating its prediction with respect to an input can be intentional. Turning off gradient recording would prevent that calculation.

exercise.prompt: A scalar parameter \(w\) has gradient 3 after one backward pass. A second independent loss contributes gradient 5, with no zeroing in between. What will w.grad contain?
exercise.answer: It contains 8 because backward accumulates gradients. That is useful for deliberate gradient accumulation, but wrong if each batch is supposed to produce an independent optimizer step.

takeaways: Autograd differentiates executed operations.
Evaluation mode and disabled gradient recording are separate controls.

title: A PyTorch module connects trainable state to computation
summary: Use registered parameters and submodules so optimization, device movement, and checkpoints see the same model.

sections.title: Forward code is only half a model
paragraphs: A model needs both a computation and an inventory of persistent state. nn.Module provides that inventory. Assigning a child module as an attribute registers it; assigning an nn.Parameter registers a trainable tensor. The forward method describes how inputs use those objects. This separation lets the same model participate in optimization, serialization, device transfers, and training or evaluation mode changes without manually maintaining several inconsistent parameter lists.

sections.title: Follow registration through a small layer
paragraphs: A linear layer contains a weight matrix and usually a bias. If you create them as ordinary tensors, they may participate in arithmetic but will not automatically appear in model.parameters(). Wrap trainable tensors in nn.Parameter or use an existing layer. Use ModuleList for a variable collection of layers; a plain Python list does not register its contents as child modules. Register nontrainable persistent state, such as a fixed lookup table, as a buffer when appropriate.

sections.title: Call the module, not forward directly
paragraphs: Invoking model(x) runs the module's call machinery around forward, including hooks. Calling model.forward(x) directly bypasses parts of that machinery. Avoid creating a new trainable layer inside every forward call: it starts with fresh weights and may not belong to the optimizer. Inspect named_parameters(), parameter counts, and state_dict() after construction. A small model with one deliberately changed parameter is a useful check that saving and loading preserve the expected state.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Compare the network-building tutorial with the Module reference's inventory of registered state. The Affine example has two parameters because assigning nn.Parameter objects as attributes registers them. A useful audit is to list their names, move the module to another dtype, and examine its state dictionary. These operations should refer to the same intended model state, rather than to unrelated collections maintained by hand.

Now contrast a Python list of layers with ModuleList. Both can hold callable objects and produce numerical outputs, so a forward pass alone does not demonstrate correct registration. Registration determines whether framework traversal finds those children for parameter collection and mode changes. The Module reference also explains why model(x) matters: call hooks surround forward execution. This is especially relevant when instrumentation or debugging depends on hooks; bypassing them can make an otherwise plausible experiment report incomplete observations.

exercise.prompt: A network stores layers in self.layers = [Linear(4,4), Linear(4,4)]. Why might its optimizer miss them, and what should replace the list?
exercise.answer: A plain list does not register child modules. Use nn.ModuleList for layers that will be called manually, or nn.Sequential when their computation is a simple chain. Registration exposes their parameters and propagates mode and device changes.

takeaways: Trainable state must be registered.
Construct layers once, then reuse them during forward passes.

title: A batch is a modeling decision as well as a speed optimization
summary: Build a data pipeline that preserves examples, labels, lengths, and padding semantics.

sections.title: Separate retrieving examples from grouping them
paragraphs: A Dataset defines how to access an example; a DataLoader controls iteration, batching, shuffling, and worker processes. This separation keeps data semantics independent of performance settings. Before adding parallel loading, inspect several examples directly and verify their labels, units, and preprocessing. A fast loader that swaps a label mapping or applies an evaluation transform incorrectly can invalidate every later experiment while producing plausible tensor shapes.

sections.title: Variable lengths need an explicit policy
paragraphs: Three token sequences of lengths 3, 5, and 2 cannot be stacked directly into one rectangular tensor. A collation function can pad them to length 5, producing \([3, 5]\) token IDs plus lengths or a validity mask. Padding values are placeholders, not observations. Attention should avoid reading them, and loss reduction should exclude them. Alternatively, bucketing similar lengths reduces wasted computation without changing the model's maximum supported context.

sections.title: Reproducibility includes the input order
paragraphs: Shuffling changes minibatch composition and therefore the optimization trajectory. Worker processes and random augmentations introduce additional sources of randomness. Record seeds and sampler settings, and distinguish throughput experiments from changes to the training distribution. Drop-last behavior can discard examples, while an iterable dataset requires careful worker sharding to avoid duplicates. Check one epoch's sample IDs when data repetition or missing examples would affect conclusions.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read the basic data tutorial for the separation between examples and batches, then use torch.utils.data for the detailed collation and worker rules. With lengths \([2, 4, 3]\), a rectangular representation allocates twelve positions but contains only nine observations. The tensor shape, attention-validity mask, and loss-validity mask describe different aspects of that representation. For next-token prediction, identify valid shifted targets explicitly rather than blindly reusing an input-length count.

The iterable-dataset examples are particularly relevant to streaming corpora. Multiple workers can each receive a dataset replica, so independent iteration without sharding may repeat the same examples. Inspect sample identifiers across one small epoch before increasing worker count. Likewise, changing drop_last can change which observations contribute to an update. A throughput improvement should be reported separately from any simultaneous change in sample exposure, padding policy, or randomness; otherwise the comparison no longer isolates pipeline speed.

exercise.prompt: Sequences have lengths \([2, 4, 3]\). How many padded positions are introduced when batching to the longest length, and how many positions should contribute to a token-averaged loss?
exercise.answer: The rectangular batch has \(3\cdot4=12\) positions. The sequences contain \(2 + 4 + 3 = 9\) real positions, so three are padding. The loss denominator should count nine valid positions, or the appropriate valid shifted targets for next-token training.

takeaways: Padding requires matching attention and loss masks.
Loader configuration can change which examples training actually sees.

title: The training loop is a controlled sequence of state changes
summary: Trace one optimizer step from data to gradients and keep evaluation behavior explicit.

sections.title: Name what changes at each stage
paragraphs: A training iteration computes predictions, measures their disagreement with targets, differentiates that loss, and updates parameters. The ordering matters because gradients accumulate and optimizer state evolves. Writing the loop yourself makes hidden assumptions visible: which examples belong to a step, how losses are averaged, when gradients are cleared, and which parameters are eligible to change. These details are part of the experiment, not merely framework syntax.

sections.title: Make one independent update
paragraphs: For an ordinary single-batch update, clear old gradients, run the model, compute a scalar loss, backpropagate, and step the optimizer. Put the model in training mode so dropout and normalization behave appropriately. For evaluation, switch to eval mode and disable gradient recording. If accumulating several microbatches, scale losses consistently with the desired effective batch mean and step only after the intended accumulation window.

sections.title: Verify a tiny problem before scaling
paragraphs: Try overfitting a small, fixed batch. If the loss cannot fall on a handful of examples, inspect labels, shapes, learning rate, frozen parameters, and gradient flow before adding more data. Aggregate reported losses using the correct number of examples or valid tokens, especially when final batches differ in size. Keep validation data outside optimizer updates, and restore training mode after validation so the next epoch does not silently use evaluation behavior.
sections.code:
model.train()
for x, y in loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    logits = model(x)
    loss = criterion(logits, y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the optimization tutorial to identify the state transition at each line of the loop: clearing gradients, computing predictions, constructing a loss, differentiating, and updating parameters. Keep those roles separate when adding accumulation. Four equal microbatch means divided by four produce the gradient of their average, provided all four computations evaluate the intended objective at the same parameters. An optimizer step between them changes that objective's evaluation points.

Consult the BatchNorm documentation before calling this an exact large-batch substitute. Batch statistics can change the forward values when the same examples are partitioned differently, so correct loss scaling cannot restore the missing full-batch statistics. Dropout realizations and other stochastic choices can also differ. For a clean verification, first use a deterministic model without batch-dependent operations, then add the actual architecture's components one at a time. Matching gradients on the simple case establishes the bookkeeping, not universal architectural equivalence.

exercise.prompt: You average four microbatch losses of equal size to emulate one larger batch. Should you backpropagate each unscaled loss, or divide each by four first?
exercise.answer: Divide each by four before backward if the goal is the mean loss over the combined batch. Otherwise the accumulated gradient is four times larger. Unequal microbatch sizes require weighting by valid examples or tokens instead of a simple factor of four. Matching a single large-batch gradient also requires the same per-example forward computation: training-mode BatchNorm changes its statistics across microbatches, and stochastic operations need consistent realizations. Loss scaling alone does not guarantee identical updates.

takeaways: Loss reduction defines the scale of an update.
A small-batch overfit check isolates basic training failures.

title: A checkpoint should restore an experiment, not just a tensor list
summary: Distinguish inference weights from the state required to resume training reproducibly.

sections.title: Different recovery goals need different state
paragraphs: For inference, restore the architecture, learned parameters, and persistent model buffers, together with matching preprocessing and evaluation mode. BatchNorm running statistics are one example of non-parameter state that can affect predictions. Resuming training requires more: optimizer moments, schedule position, mixed-precision scaler state when used, and the current training step. A checkpoint that restores weights but resets those components starts a related experiment rather than continuing the same trajectory. Decide the recovery goal before a long job begins.

sections.title: Save named state with its context
paragraphs: A model state_dict normally maps parameter and persistent-buffer names to tensors; modules can also define extra state. An optimizer state_dict has a different structure, containing per-parameter state and parameter-group settings. Save model and optimizer state dictionaries alongside configuration, tokenizer or preprocessing versions, and a data identifier. For closer reproduction, record random-number-generator states and the sampler position. Exact continuation across different hardware or library versions may still be unavailable because kernels and numerical behavior can differ. Store the checkpoint format version so future code can interpret it deliberately.

sections.title: Test the restore path early
paragraphs: Save a small run, construct a fresh model and optimizer, load state, and compare predictions before proceeding. For a resume test, compare the next update with an uninterrupted run under controlled deterministic settings. Write checkpoints atomically where possible so interruption does not leave a half-written file. Keep a previous known-good copy. Loading serialized objects can have security implications, so use trusted checkpoints and the framework's restricted loading options appropriate to the file format.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: The saving-and-loading guide distinguishes a model state dictionary from a general training checkpoint. Inspect a BatchNorm-containing model to see persistent running statistics alongside learned parameters. Inspect Adam separately to see optimizer state and parameter-group configuration. These are different structures with different purposes, so a generic instruction to save the weights is too ambiguous when a later reader needs to reproduce predictions or continue optimization.

A useful restore comparison has two stages. First, load into a fresh architecture and compare evaluation outputs on identical inputs and preprocessing. Second, restore optimizer and other training state, then compare the next update against an uninterrupted run. The second stage is stricter: identical predictions before the step do not prove identical moment estimates or schedule positions. For stochastic data pipelines, also account for sample order and random state. Cross-version or cross-device bitwise identity is a separate requirement that a state dictionary alone cannot establish.

exercise.prompt: Two runs load identical weights, but one restores Adam state and the other initializes Adam from scratch. Must their next updates match if the next batch is the same?
exercise.answer: No. The restored run uses accumulated first and second moments and its existing step count; the fresh optimizer does not. Matching weights and data do not imply matching optimizer updates or future trajectories.

takeaways: Inference restoration and training continuation require different state.
A checkpoint is useful only after its restore path has been tested.

title: GPU memory belongs to live tensors and asynchronous work
summary: Understand device placement, transfers, and allocated versus reserved memory before diagnosing CUDA behavior.

sections.title: The CPU and GPU have separate jobs
paragraphs: The CPU often prepares data and launches operations, while the GPU executes many tensor kernels. A tensor's device identifies where its storage lives. Moving a model does not automatically move every external input, and moving a tensor returns a result that must be used. Device mismatches are usually ownership mistakes: model parameters, inputs, targets, and newly created helper tensors need a compatible placement policy.

sections.title: Separate memory categories
paragraphs: GPU memory holds parameters, gradients, optimizer state, saved activations, and temporary workspace. PyTorch's caching allocator can reserve memory after a tensor is freed so later allocations are fast. Allocated memory tracks live tensor allocations; reserved memory includes cached blocks. A high number in a system monitor therefore does not prove that all of it is occupied by currently useful tensors. CPU-to-GPU transfers can also become a bottleneck when kernels are short.

sections.title: Measure asynchronous operations correctly
paragraphs: CUDA launches are typically asynchronous with respect to the CPU. Timing only the Python call can measure launch overhead rather than completed GPU work. Synchronize at measurement boundaries or use CUDA events, while avoiding unnecessary synchronization in the normal training path. Pinned host memory and nonblocking copies can help overlap transfers in suitable pipelines, but they are not universal speed switches. Measure end-to-end throughput, and create small helper tensors on the input's device.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Read CUDA Semantics as a guide to ownership and execution boundaries. Device movement answers where a tensor's data resides; the allocator statistics answer which allocations PyTorch currently uses or manages. Neither is identical to a system monitor's total process footprint. A debugging record should distinguish allocated bytes, reserved bytes, and the stage of the iteration at which each measurement was taken.

The asynchronous-execution discussion explains why a host-side timer around a kernel launch can be misleading. Decide whether the measurement concerns one kernel, a batch, or complete request latency, then place synchronization at the boundaries needed for that question. Excess synchronization inside normal execution can destroy useful overlap and create a different workload. Pinned memory and nonblocking transfers are mechanisms to investigate, not promised speedups. Their value depends on actual transfer sizes, stream coordination, available overlap, and the rest of the pipeline.

exercise.prompt: After deleting a large tensor, allocated memory drops but reserved memory stays high. Is that evidence of a leak? What observation would be more concerning?
exercise.answer: Not by itself: the allocator may retain freed blocks for reuse. A repeated increase in allocated memory across otherwise identical iterations suggests live tensors or graphs are being retained and deserves investigation.

takeaways: Device placement should be explicit and consistent.
Reserved memory and live tensor memory are different measurements.

title: Mixed precision trades numerical resolution for efficiency
summary: Use FP32, FP16, and BF16 with an understanding of exponent range, rounding, and gradient scaling.

sections.title: Fewer bits change two kinds of resolution
paragraphs: A floating-point format allocates bits to sign, exponent, and fraction. Exponent range determines how large or small representable magnitudes can be; fraction bits determine precision within that range. FP16 and BF16 both use 16 bits, but BF16 has a wider exponent range and fewer fraction bits. Neither is simply a smaller, exact version of FP32. The best format depends on the operations, hardware, and numerical sensitivity of the workload.

sections.title: Use precision per operation
paragraphs: Automatic mixed precision chooses lower precision for suitable operations and retains higher precision where needed. Autocast should cover the forward computation and loss construction, rather than indiscriminately converting every tensor. FP16 training often uses gradient scaling: multiply the loss to protect small gradients from underflow, then unscale before applying updates or gradient clipping. BF16's range often removes that need, although rounding and unstable computations still require attention.

sections.title: Check accuracy as well as throughput
paragraphs: Mixed precision can reduce activation memory and speed suitable matrix operations, but gains depend on model size, dimensions, and hardware support. A tiny model dominated by Python overhead may barely improve. Compare a fixed-batch loss and short learning curve with an FP32 reference, then measure complete training throughput. If gradients become nonfinite, inspect the loss and input ranges before assuming a different dtype alone will fix the underlying instability.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Follow the AMP recipe's ordering of autocast, scaled backward, unscaling, clipping, and optimizer stepping. The clipping example here isolates why the order matters: multiplying the loss changes recorded gradient magnitudes without changing the desired unscaled objective. A norm threshold applied before that scale is removed acts on a different numerical quantity. Reading a training script line by line is more informative than seeing that it contains an autocast context somewhere.

Precision choices also need a numerical baseline. Compare selected activations, loss values, and gradients against an FP32 computation before interpreting a throughput result. BF16's wider exponent range addresses a different problem from fractional precision, so fewer overflows do not guarantee equally accurate arithmetic. The recipe's speed claims are hardware- and workload-dependent; a CPU run cannot validate a CUDA kernel's benefit. Keep correctness checks, memory measurements, and wall-clock measurements separate so each result supports only the claim it actually tests.

exercise.prompt: Why should gradient clipping happen after unscaling FP16 gradients? What error occurs if a norm threshold of 1 is applied to gradients scaled by 1024?
exercise.answer: Clipping should act on the real gradient. Before unscaling, the norm is inflated by 1024, so applying threshold 1 can shrink the eventual unscaled gradient toward a norm of \(\frac1{1024}\) instead of 1, making updates unnecessarily small.

takeaways: Exponent range and fractional precision are separate properties.
Unscale before operations that inspect the true gradient magnitude.

title: Debug the first broken invariant
summary: Investigate NaNs, exploding gradients, and out-of-memory errors by locating the earliest abnormal state.

sections.title: The visible failure may be downstream
paragraphs: A NaN loss can originate in invalid inputs, an unstable operation, an excessive update, or corrupted optimizer state. An out-of-memory error may appear in a harmless final operation because earlier code retained computation graphs. Start by reproducing the failure on the smallest fixed batch and recording the first step where behavior changes. Change one suspected cause at a time so that a successful run actually explains the failure.

sections.title: Check the forward and backward boundaries
paragraphs: Inspect finite values and reasonable ranges in inputs, logits, loss, gradients, and parameters. A logarithm of zero or normalization by a nearly zero denominator can create nonfinite values before backward begins. Exploding gradients can be controlled with clipping, but persistent explosion may signal poor scaling or an unsuitable learning rate. Compare with FP32 and temporarily disable optional components to isolate the responsible operation without rewriting the whole model.

sections.title: Look for retained graphs when memory grows
paragraphs: Appending a loss tensor to a list keeps graph references reachable; logging a detached scalar avoids that ownership. Ordinary backward frees most saved activations, so graph references alone do not prove a large leak. Retaining graphs for later backward or storing intermediate activations can be much more expensive. Emptying the CUDA cache does not free live tensors. If memory is stable but insufficient, reduce batch or sequence length; if it grows, trace retained references and graph lifetimes.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: Use the autograd and CUDA references together to distinguish a live graph from unused allocator memory. A differentiable loss stored in a list keeps a Python-visible connection to graph nodes. Whether that retains large saved activations depends on backward and graph-retention behavior. By contrast, reserved but unused CUDA blocks can persist even after their tensors are no longer live. These mechanisms require different evidence and different fixes.

Construct a short diagnostic trace over repeated identical iterations: record live allocation after forward, after backward, and after dropping temporary references. Increasing memory at the same boundary is more suspicious than a single high peak. For nonfinite values, move the trace earlier through inputs, logits, loss, gradients, and updated parameters until the first invalid state appears. Gradient clipping cannot repair a NaN already created by an invalid forward operation, and empty_cache cannot release tensors still owned by application code.

exercise.prompt: Training code stores losses.append(loss) and retains the associated graphs for later backward passes, even though the list is intended only for logging. What is the likely memory problem and the minimal logging fix?
exercise.answer: The history unnecessarily owns differentiable losses and their retained graphs, including saved activations needed for later backward. Store loss.detach().item() for scalar logs instead, and keep graph retention only where the training algorithm actually requires it. A normal backward frees most saved activations, so investigate other references if growth remains.

takeaways: Find the earliest nonfinite value or unexpected allocation.
Caching cleanup cannot release tensors that are still referenced.

title: Experiment tracking should make comparisons reconstructable
summary: Log the evidence needed to connect a result to its data, code, configuration, and resource budget.

sections.title: A curve without context is an anecdote
paragraphs: A loss plot is useful only if you know what produced it. Track the code revision, dataset version, split definition, seed, model configuration, optimizer settings, and hardware context alongside metrics. TensorBoard and W&B provide interfaces for organizing such records, but the scientific value comes from choosing comparable measurements. A tracker cannot infer that one run used twice as much data or a different validation prompt.

sections.title: Choose a meaningful horizontal axis
paragraphs: Optimizer step, processed examples, processed tokens, and wall-clock time answer different questions. Two runs with different batch sizes may look similar against steps while consuming very different compute. Log validation metrics with an explicit split name and aggregation rule. For a variable-length language task, token-weighted loss is not generally equal to the mean of per-batch means. Keep enough raw information to reconstruct the comparison.

sections.title: Record failures and artifacts too
paragraphs: Save representative predictions, error categories, checkpoints, and configuration snapshots rather than retaining only the best scalar score. Mark interrupted or diverged runs so they do not silently disappear from a comparison. Avoid logging every large tensor on every step, which can create overhead and storage costs. Separate configuration chosen before a run from notes added afterward, and preserve links between a reported result and its exact checkpoint.

sections.title: Reading the original source
paragraphs: The TensorBoard tutorial demonstrates how a scalar is attached to a tag and a step. Treat those fields as part of the measurement definition. A tag such as validation/loss should identify the evaluated split and reduction, while the horizontal coordinate should identify optimizer steps, examples, tokens, or time. Reusing a tag for a different denominator can make two curves appear comparable even when their values answer different questions.

Extend the example with unequal final batches: a batch of ten observations and a batch of one observation should not receive equal weight when reporting a per-observation mean. Log enough counts to reconstruct the aggregate, alongside the source revision and configuration. The interface records values; it cannot establish that preprocessing, label mapping, or evaluation prompts match across runs. Link a reported result to a particular checkpoint and dataset version so a later inspection can recover the experiment behind the visualization.

exercise.prompt: Run A uses 32 examples per optimizer step and run B uses 128. Both reach a score after 1,000 steps. What additional axes help compare them fairly?
exercise.answer: A processed 32,000 examples while B processed 128,000, assuming full batches. Compare against examples or tokens processed, wall-clock time, and an appropriate compute estimate, and report whether the number of unique examples and epochs also differ.

takeaways: Log enough context to reconstruct a comparison.
Steps, data exposure, and elapsed time are different budgets.
